analysis.one_liner: Bans members of Congress, the President, and the Vice President from owning or trading individual stocks.
analysis.headline: The Senate Homeland Security Committee approved the stock-trading ban in December 2024 and placed it on the Senate calendar, but the full Senate never voted on it before the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would bar members of Congress, the President, and the Vice President, along with their spouses and dependent children, from buying or selling individual stocks, commodities, futures, and digital assets. Holdings would have to be sold or placed in a blind trust, with violations drawing fines equal to a month's pay or 10 percent of the un-sold investment each month. It would also impose a $500 fine for each missed transaction report and require financial disclosures to be filed electronically in a searchable public database. The Senate committee with jurisdiction approved it, but no floor vote ever happened.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary Americans, in the form of a Congress that does not hold individual stocks in companies it can regulate, subsidize, or investigate. Financial disclosure would also become searchable online instead of buried in paper filings.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Ordinary Americans relying on impartial lawmaking

how_it_helps.text: Members of Congress, the President, and the Vice President, plus spouses and dependent children, could no longer buy or sell individual stocks, commodities, futures, or digital assets, eliminating the conflict between personal portfolios and public duties [S2][S3].

Existing holdings would have to be divested or placed in a blind trust within 120 days of the effective date, and violations would draw a monthly civil penalty equal to the greater of one month's pay or 10 percent of the value of each un-sold investment [S3].

Failure to file a required transaction report under the STOCK Act would carry an automatic $500 fine, and all financial disclosures would have to be filed electronically and searchable by the public online, including by asset and ticker symbol [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Members of Congress and their families, who would have to sell or blind-trust their individual stock holdings, and wealth management firms that earn fees managing those portfolios. Diversified index funds, Treasury securities, and municipal bonds would remain allowed, so no one would be forced out of savings entirely.
analysis.who_pays_short: Members of Congress with stock portfolios

drawbacks.text: The reported version delayed the effective date to March 31, 2027, meaning the ban would not apply until after the next Congress had begun [S3].
Spousal compensation carve-outs would still let a member's spouse keep securities received as pay or board compensation from their own employer, leaving a channel for family stock ownership [S3].

Enforcement rests on congressional ethics offices imposing civil fines, with no criminal penalty and no independent prosecutor, which critics could argue leaves compliance dependent on self-policing [S3].

Members with hard-to-sell private or illiquid investments would get up to 150 days of extensions, and family trusts could be exempted if the member has no control over the trustee, creating exceptions an honest supporter would have to acknowledge [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — removing the personal financial stake of lawmakers in the laws they write — is large for public trust and conflicts of interest, and the cost falls almost entirely on the officials being regulated. The main design weaknesses are the delayed effective date, the spousal carve-outs, and reliance on ethics offices for enforcement rather than criminal penalties.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate committee approved the bill and put it on the calendar for the floor, but Senate leaders never brought it up for a vote, and it died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in April 2023 by Senator Merkley with 23 cosponsors, all Democrats or independents, and was referred to the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee [S1][S4][S5].

In July 2024 the committee ordered the bill reported favorably with an amendment, and in December 2024 it formally reported the bill, which by then had been expanded to cover the President and Vice President and to include digital assets [S3][S5].

On December 19, 2024 the bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders, meaning it was ready for the full chamber to take up, but no vote was ever scheduled, and the Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Members of Congress and their families, who keep the ability to trade individual stocks while in office, along with the wealth management industry that administers those portfolios.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Members of Congress who kept trading stocks

against.name: Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a floor vote after it was reported from committee and placed on the calendar.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.role: No Republican cosponsors or floor support
against.what_they_did: None of the 49 Senate Republicans cosponsored the bill, and no floor vote was ever demanded or scheduled before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All 23 cosponsors were Democrats or independents (21 of 48 Democrats, 2 of 4 independents); no Republican signed on, and the bill never reached a floor vote.

industries.industry: Members of Congress and their families
industries.note: The bill would force them to divest individual stock holdings or blind-trust them, and impose monthly fines for noncompliance. Opposition centered on this direct interest of the officials being regulated.
The reported amendment extended the trading ban to the President and Vice President, a major expansion over the introduced bill. The bill died before it could apply.

industries.industry: Wealth management and trust administration firms
industries.note: The introduced version would have channeled members' holdings into qualified blind trusts managed by financial institutions, entrenching that business, while the reported version instead requires dissolving blind trusts and outright divestiture. Either way, diversified index fund managers would keep members' business.
